analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers erase student loans in bankruptcy like any other debt.
analysis.headline: The bill to let student borrowers discharge loans in bankruptcy sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended, despite 38 cosponsors including one Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans are one of the few debts you cannot wipe out in bankruptcy unless you prove "undue hardship," a standard so strict that most borrowers never even try. This bill would strike that exception, so federal, nonprofit, and private student loans could be discharged in bankruptcy like credit card debt or medical bills. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers in genuine financial distress — people who lose a job, face illness, or otherwise cannot pay — would regain the ability to start over through bankruptcy, the same protection available to nearly every other kind of debtor. This also catches borrowers with private student loans, which often carry high rates and few repayment protections.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the bankruptcy-code exception (11 U.S.C. 523(a)(8)) that currently makes student loans nondischargeable except in rare "undue hardship" cases [S3].

Applies to loans from governments, nonprofits, and private lenders, plus obligations to repay educational benefits, scholarships, or stipends, so the escape valve covers the full range of student debt [S2].
Applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, leaving existing court cases under the old rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and the federal loan program bear the cost: some debts they once could collect forever would instead be wiped out. Losses on federal Direct Loans are ultimately absorbed by taxpayers, and private lenders would likely charge somewhat higher rates or lend more cautiously to reflect the new risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders, the federal loan program, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Easier discharge could raise borrowing costs: lenders facing more bankruptcy risk would likely charge higher rates, and the federal government would book larger losses on loans it forgives in court, costs that taxpayers indirectly bear (policy mechanism; not in provided sources).
Some borrowers who could afford to repay might use bankruptcy to shed loans, which is why lenders argue for keeping a hardship test (policy objection; not in provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: today the "undue hardship" bar is so high that distressed borrowers rarely qualify, and this bill would give them the same fresh start the bankruptcy code gives everyone else. The costs — somewhat higher loan rates for future borrowers and losses to the federal loan portfolio — are real but modest compared with the harm of trapping people in unpayable debt for life. The main design question is whether the bill goes too far by removing any hardship test entirely rather than loosening it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on May 4, 2017, with nine original cosponsors including Republican Rep. John Katko [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on June 7, 2017 to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor and died at the end of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill drew 38 cosponsors, 37 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student lenders and the federal loan collection operation keep the current rule that student debts can rarely be discharged, while borrowers in severe distress remain unable to use bankruptcy to escape them.

for.name: Rep. John K. Delaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.

for.name: Rep. John Katko
for.what_they_did: Was one of nine original cosponsors, the only Republican, lending the bill a bipartisan sponsor list.

for.name: 37 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 38 House members.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat in committee and on a subcommittee referral until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors but one were Democrats (37 D, 1 R), and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Under current law their loans are nearly impossible to discharge, guaranteeing collection for decades; the bill would restore bankruptcy risk, and lenders' interest in keeping that shield runs directly against distressed borrowers who want a fresh start.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Their revenue depends on collecting loans for life; discharge in bankruptcy would end some of those income streams. Their preference for the status quo conflicts with borrowers seeking relief.

The government would collect less on Direct Loans that get discharged, with losses ultimately borne by taxpayers; in exchange, borrowers in hardship get the same bankruptcy protection as other debtors. The program's fiscal interest in full repayment runs against distressed borrowers.
